HCV infection is a major risk factor for the development of ALD and the progression of fibrosis in alcoholic patients, and that HCV infection may also be associated with an increased risk of developing ALD in non-alcoholic patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the hepatitis C virus (HCV) in the progression of alcoholic cirrhosis.
the role of HCV in the pathogenesis of liver disease in alcoholics.

the development of a new generation of materials for the treatment of liver disease, with the ultimate aim of developing a drug delivery system that will be capable of delivering a drug directly into the diseased liver, in a controlled and safe manner.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
alcohol is the most important risk factor for the development of alcoholic liver cirrhosis, and that alcohol and hepatitis C virus are the most important risk factors for the development of HCC.
the presence of HCV in the liver of patients with alcoholic cirrhosis is not a prerequisite for progression to liver failure.
the presence of hepatitis C virus (HCV) in patients with alcoholic liver disease (ALD) is not associated with the progression of ALD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HCV is a significant risk factor in the development of ALD and the progression from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis.
we are trying to understand the mechanisms of liver damage in alcoholic liver disease and how they are influenced by the hepatitis C virus.

the contribution of hepatitis C virus (HCV) to the progression of alcohol-induced liver injury (ALD) is not well understood and that it is difficult to determine the relative contributions of HCV and alcohol to the development of liver disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have identified a novel role for the hepatitis C virus in the development of alcoholic liver disease, which is a major cause of liver-related death worldwide.
we have identified a new class of compounds that can be used to treat liver fibrosis.

the presence of HCV infection, especially in the absence of alcohol, may have a protective effect against the development of alcoholic liver disease and that HCV is not a cofactor for the development of alcoholic cirrhosis.
